explain.say: When you put cans, bottles, paper and boxes into one recycling bin, who sorts them all? A giant machine! Look at the board. Everything is tipped onto a conveyor belt, and workers first pull out things that shouldn't be there, like plastic bags that tangle the machines.

explain.say: See the spinning discs? Flat paper and cardboard ride over the top of the spinning disc screen, like surfing, while bottles and cans tumble down through the gaps. Glass usually breaks and falls through too. Why do you think flat things stay on top?

explain.say: Now look at the magnet. Steel cans contain iron, so a strong magnet lifts them off the belt. But aluminium drink cans aren't magnetic! So, at the coil, fast-spinning magnets make electric currents in the aluminium that push it, and the cans jump off into their own bin.

explain.say: See the air jet? A light sensor shines on each plastic item and works out what kind of plastic it is from the light that bounces back. In a split second, a puff of air blows it into the right chute. Can you find the recycling number on a plastic bottle at home?

explain.say: Amazing, right? At the end, see the bales: each material is squashed into big blocks and sent to factories to become new cans, boxes and bottles. Well done! Wow: recycling an aluminium can saves about 95 percent of the energy needed to make one from new metal!

faq.q: How does a recycling plant sort mixed recycling?
faq.a: On conveyor belts, using people and machines together: spinning screens for paper, magnets for steel, eddy currents for aluminium, and light sensors with air jets for plastics.
Disc screens with spinning, star-shaped wheels carry flat paper and cardboard over the top, while round bottles and cans fall through the gaps.
asks: How is paper sorted in recycling?

faq.q: How are steel and aluminium cans separated?
faq.a: A magnet lifts out steel cans because they contain iron. Aluminium isn't magnetic, so a spinning magnet called an eddy current separator pushes aluminium cans off the belt.
asks: Why are aluminium cans not magnetic?

faq.a: Optical sorters shine light on each item and read which type of plastic it is from the reflected light. A quick puff of air then blows it into the right chute.
asks: How is plastic sorted for recycling?

faq.q: Why should I rinse my recycling?
faq.a: Food and liquid can soak into paper and spoil whole batches, and dirty items may be rejected. A quick rinse helps more get recycled.

facts: Recycling aluminium uses about 95% less energy than making it from raw ore.
Eddy current separators use a fast-changing magnetic field to push aluminium out of a mixed stream.

quiz.say: How are steel cans picked out of mixed recycling?
quiz.show: How are steel cans picked out of mixed recycling?
quiz.why: Steel contains iron, which a magnet attracts.

wrong.1: Air jets are used for plastics, not steel.
wrong.2: Steel cans are sorted by magnetism, not floating.

quiz.say: Why can't an ordinary magnet pick up aluminium cans?
quiz.show: Why can't an ordinary magnet pick up aluminium cans?
quiz.why: Aluminium is not attracted to magnets, so eddy currents are used.

wrong.1: Weight isn't the problem; a magnet can lift light iron things.
wrong.2: Paint doesn't stop a magnet attracting iron.
